Following his 2023-2024 performance evaluation using the state-approved Collins and Blaha superintendent evaluation tool, the Board rated him "highly effective." The item cites accomplishments including bond progress, a new high school pre-internship program, top-of-state student achievement, successful union negotiations, and state-funding advocacy. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Item 6.D., a personnel consideration titled "Superintendent's Contract Extension," presented at the Troy Board of Education's regular meeting on August 20, 2024. The Board reported it had recently completed Superintendent Dr. Richard Machesky's performance evaluation and used the item to share its assessment with the community. Using the state-approved Collins and Blaha superintendent evaluation tool, the Board reviewed Dr. Machesky's work performance over the 2023-2024 school year and awarded him a rating of "highly effective." The statement praises him for continuing to lead the district with distinction and strategic focus.

The Board noted that his superior development of subordinate administrators had cost the district some key employees who accepted career advancements in other school districts, while his reputation as a skilled mentor helped the district recruit bright, ambitious replacements. Specific accomplishments cited include: bond work progressing with ease; the launch of a highly successful pre-internship program for high school students, built on the strong connections he has fostered for years with area business leaders and the Troy Foundation; student achievement remaining at the top of the state; successful guidance of contract negotiations with all of the district's union groups; and lobbying efforts for state funding that resulted in Troy receiving nearly double the increase initially recommended by the Governor. The Board also recognized his exemplary model of ethical behavior and kindness, concluding that it was appropriate to extend his contract through June 30, 2029.

The recommended action was acceptance of a resolution: "BE IT THEREFORE RESOLVED that the Troy Board of Education extends the contract of the Superintendent of Schools as mentioned above. This contract will be in effect from July 1, 2024 through June 30, 2029, without tenure in the administrative position and subject to provisions of the written Agreement." The suggested resolution includes Moved by, Supported by, and Yes/No vote fields, which are blank in the extracted text, so the recorded vote is not captured here. The document functions both as a contractual action — a five-year extension of the superintendent's term — and as a public performance narrative justifying the renewal.

The memo requests approval to purchase the iPads needed for the annual device refresh for the 2024/25 school year.

It explains that under the district's K-12 1:1 adoption program, students receive iPads at three grade-entry points — kindergarten, 4th grade, and 9th grade. Item 8.C. under Business at the Troy Board of Education's August 20, 2024 regular meeting, a consideration titled "Serving Lines – Barnard, Bemis and Hamilton Elementary Schools." The item states that the cafeteria serving lines at Barnard, Bemis, and Hamilton Elementaries are in need of replacement. Competitive pricing was obtained through the MOR Commodity & Commercial Food Purchasing Cooperative, and the pricing was compared and reviewed by Gayle Moran, the district's Food Service Liaison.

The recommended action is acceptance of the resolution: "Be it therefore resolved that the purchase of serving lines be awarded to Great Lakes Hotel Supply in the amount of $141,014.71 and that this amount be approved as an expenditure of the Food Service Fund." The suggested resolution provides Moved By, Supported By, and Yes/No fields, which are blank in the extracted text, so the recorded vote is not captured here. The purchase is funded entirely from the district's Food Service Fund and represents a food-service capital replacement across three elementary buildings, procured through a purchasing cooperative rather than through a standalone competitive bid.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
The Troy School District Cash Position Report for the month ended June 30, 2024 presents the district's cash balances and monthly cash flow across four fund groups: General (funds 101, 120, 122), Special Revenue (520, 529, 530, 531), Debt Service (315, 316, 320, 321) and Capital Projects (419, 423, 498, 499).

Opening and closing balances. Total cash across all funds began the month at $242,223,454 (May 31, 2024) and ended at $239,538,666 (June 30, 2024), a net decrease of about $2.68 million. By fund, ending balances were: General $38,165,968 (down from $40,997,076); Special Revenue $11,517,578 (up from $10,797,074); Debt Service $2,625,343 (up from $2,521,710); and Capital Projects $187,229,778 (down from $187,907,594). The Capital Projects balance dominates total district cash, reflecting unspent bond proceeds.

Revenues received during June totaled $18,433,760. The largest component was State Aid of $12,472,296 ($11,309,597 to the General Fund and $1,162,699 to Special Revenue). Federal grant revenue was $1,895,387 ($1,096,676 General; $798,711 Special Revenue). Local revenue totaled $2,861,075 ($2,557,807 General; $303,268 Special Revenue). Interest income received totaled $1,205,000, distributed as $269,635 (General), $103,633 (Debt Service) and $831,733 (Capital Projects). No bond proceeds, state grant revenue, property tax revenue, sale of property, or transfers were recorded for the month.

Expenditures during June totaled $21,118,548. These comprised accounts payable of $8,884,257 ($6,278,413 General, $1,096,295 Special Revenue, $1,509,549 Capital Projects); payroll of $4,989,465 ($4,541,585 General, $447,880 Special Revenue); and payroll tax and ORS (Office of Retirement Services) withholdings of $7,244,826, all charged to the General Fund. No bond payments or transfers out were recorded.

Because June expenditures ($21.1 million) exceeded revenues received ($18.4 million) by roughly $2.7 million, total cash declined for the month, driven mainly by the General Fund, which absorbed $18,064,824 of expenditures against $15,233,715 of revenues received. The report is a supporting schedule within the monthly Treasurer's Report to the Board of Education and provides board members a liquidity snapshot by fund group.

As a year-end unaudited statement, these figures precede the district's annual independent audit and were presented within the Business Services materials for the August 20, 2024 Board of Education meeting.

Consent agenda. Hauff, Secretary, Troy Board of Education (notation "GH/jh").

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A 'Summer Professional Learning Update' delivered at the Troy Board of Education Workshop on September 3, 2024, reporting on the professional-development activities the Troy School District conducted over summer 2024 under its 'OneTroy' framework. The stated objective is 'Building Capacity' - to provide professional learning opportunities for staff, community, and students throughout OneTroy.

The presentation catalogs the summer's 'OneTroy Summer Learning' offerings: Summer Curriculum Development; an Administrative Kick-Off Meeting; the Universal Design for Learning (UDL) Conference; the TSD Math and Literacy Project; a Pre-K Institute; Troy Institutes K-12; New Teacher Orientation; Future Ready Learning Environments; and Welcome Back Week.

Several programs are detailed. The UDL Conference was a two-day event attended by 3 secondary administrators and 2 CIS (curriculum and instructional staff); the slide cites UDL's founding premise that 'barriers to learning occur in the interaction with the curriculum - they are not inherent solely in the capacity of the learner,' so that when education fails, the curriculum rather than the learner should take responsibility for adaptation. The TSD Literacy Project engaged over 80 teachers across grade bands K-2, 3-5, 6-8, and 9-10, focused on 'Sustaining the Workshop Method PreK-10' and responsive teaching. Principal Meetings and the Admin Kick-Off had leaders reflect on the current state and next steps to sustain vision work, review the district's Mission, Vision, Values and Thematic Goals, and hold level-specific meetings tied to bond engagement and communication materials. Future Ready Learning Environments involved 55 educators in grades K-5 in a teacher-led effort focused on student learning. New Teacher Orientation was a four-day professional development spanning each department, including a tour of the district and time with mentor teachers. Finally, the Staff Welcome Back / August Learning featured a keynote speaker, choice sessions, MTSS work at the secondary level, and department time.

The deck is informational, describing participation counts and program design rather than budget figures, votes, or resolutions. Its through-line is how the summer's professional learning reinforced district priorities - literacy and math instruction, universal design, future-ready environments, and vision alignment including bond-related communication - heading into the 2024-2025 school year.

What it is
A Board of Education workshop presentation (September 3, 2024) on Troy School District's communication strategies across three levels - District, School, and Troy.

Framework
- General strategy: focused communication (goal + audience), prioritized messaging (Must, Should, Could, Want, Wish), timeframe, organizational priorities (finances, culture, staffing), supporting data, and a feedback/audit/revise loop

Tools

- Attendance Area Review - engaging Plante Moran, forming a community committee, and communicating outcomes
- New Smith Middle School - bond passage, renderings, groundbreaking, moving and transportation plans, grand opening, and feedback loop

Purpose
Shows the board the district's approach to strategic communications.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A 'Communication Strategies' presentation delivered at the Troy Board of Education Workshop on September 3, 2024, describing how the Troy School District approaches communication at the District, School, and Troy-community levels.

The deck opens with 'General Comms Strategies,' a planning framework built around: focused communication (defining the goal - e.g., create awareness or attract new families); audience (families, students, Oakland County, legislative, etc.); prioritized communication using a Must/Should/Could/Want/Wish scale; timeframe (now, next week, all year long); organizational priorities (the year's 'big rocks,' finances, culture, staffing); supporting data (analytics, surveys, enrollment, test scores); and a closing feedback, audit, and revise step.

It then maps key stakeholder groups, noting several iterations within each: students (including those transitioning and those with additional needs such as ELD and special education); staff (TSD staff and contracted staff); parents and families; the broader community (future families, past families, voters, and the business community tied to CTE, CAP, and internships); and government (legislators, the governor, and others).

A 'Philosophy' slide lists guiding principles: balancing two-way and one-way communication; keeping messages short and sweet; using simple, branded, well-designed materials; 'break your own bad news'; using more than one tool; recognizing audiences must see something six or more times before acting; treating social media as essential to any plan; and using high-quality photos and video to tell the story.

The 'Tools' inventory spans mass communications platforms (Blackboard/Finalsite for snow days and power outages), district-wide and school newsletters, websites, committees, email, phone calls and text messages, video, the supplemental 'Troy Times,' traditional media (TV, newspaper, radio), flyers, boards, postcards, banners, posters, the PTO and PTO Council, coffee talks, book reads, math nights, community feedback, PeachJar, and social platforms including Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, and Twitter, plus digital advertising and seasonal 'Welcome Back' and fall/spring updates.

Two case studies illustrate the approach. The Attendance Area Review Process outlines meeting with Plante Moran to determine recommendations, discussing with Cabinet, forming a committee, creating and vetting applications, selecting a cross-section of the community through district and school newsletters, holding meetings to discuss recommendations, determining direction, and communicating outcomes with a feedback loop. The second case study, the new Smith Middle School, traces the arc from needs assessment and site plan through passing a bond (using all tools), showcasing renderings on boards, website, and newsletter, a groundbreaking, the building process, communicating moving and transportation plans to Smith families and the larger community, a grand opening, and an audit/review feeding the next wave of middle-school construction communications. The presentation closes with a questions slide and contains no votes or dollar figures.

- The Oakland Community Health Network (OCHN) asked school boards throughout Oakland County to partner with it by approving the proclamation at their September board meetings.

Key points in the resolution
- World Suicide Prevention Day is observed each year on September 10.
- Suicidal thoughts can affect anyone regardless of age, gender, race, orientation, income, religion, or background.
- Per the CDC, each year more than 48,000 people die by suicide.
- Suicide is the second leading cause of death for ages 10-34, fourth for ages 35-54, and eighth for ages 55-64.
- References the National Alliance on Mental Illness (NAMI) and the 988 Suicide Prevention Lifeline.
- Notes OCHN's commitment to being a Zero Suicide organization.

Action
- Acceptance of the resolution recognizing September 2024 as National Suicide Prevention Month; includes blank Moved by / Supported by and YES/NO lines.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose: Recognition item 2.D. and suggested resolution from the September 17, 2024 regular Board of Education meeting proclaiming September 2024 as National Suicide Prevention Month. The Oakland Community Health Network (OCHN) asked school boards throughout Oakland County to partner with it by approving such a proclamation at their September board meetings, and the recommended action is acceptance of the resolution, which includes blank "Moved by" and "Supported by" lines and YES/NO tallies. The resolution's whereas clauses state that September is known as National Suicide Prevention Month, intended to help raise awareness surrounding suicide prevention resources available in the community; that World Suicide Prevention Day is observed each year on September 10; that suicidal thoughts can affect anyone regardless of age, gender, race, orientation, income level, religion, or background; that according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) each year more than 48,000 people died by suicide; and that suicide is the second leading cause of death for people 10 to 34 years of age, the fourth leading cause among people 35 to 54 years of age, and the eighth leading cause among people 55 to 64 years of age. It further notes that organizations like the National Alliance on Mental Illness (NAMI) and the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline, 988, work to help individuals in crisis and provide resources to shed light on this highly stigmatized topic, and that OCHN is committed to being a Zero Suicide organization and to cultivating a network of providers engaged in the Zero Suicide philosophy. The resolving clause states that Oakland Community Health Network hereby recognizes September 2024 as National Suicide Prevention Month and calls upon individuals, government agencies, public and private institutions, businesses, faith-based organizations, and schools to recommit the state to increasing awareness and understanding of suicide prevention and the need for appropriate and accessible services to assist individuals in crisis.

By source, the budget is Local Sources $47,455,345 (July actual $2,124,440), State Sources $126,436,088 (actual $0), Federal Sources $4,502,005 (actual $0), and Interdistrict Sources $13,151,085 (actual $0); state and federal aid had not yet posted in month one. General Fund expenditures: approved budget $195,485,356 versus July actual $2,177,213. Instruction totals $128,084,453 budget / $262,631 actual, split among Basic Programs ($94,757,497 / $169,328), Added Needs ($32,343,750 / $61,152), and Adult Education ($983,206 / $32,151). Support Services total $66,585,319 budget / $1,910,575 actual, including Pupil ($14,911,509 / $15,723), Instructional Staff ($12,379,366 / $281,993), General Administration ($2,496,767 / $138,705), School Administration ($9,925,447 / $409,702), Business Services ($2,031,116 / $89,282), Operations ($14,134,448 / $790,657), Pupil Transportation ($4,308,072 / $12,766), Central Services ($3,877,086 / $123,642), and Athletics/Other ($2,521,508 / $48,106). Community Services is $172,084 / $4,008, Debt Service $477,900 / $0, and Outgoing Transfers $165,600 / $0. The General Fund shows Revenues Over (Under) Expenditures of budgeted $(3,940,833) and July actual $(52,773).

Consolidated Debt Service Funds: revenues budget $30,860,850 (Local $30,560,850, State $300,000) versus actual $1,576,169; expenditures budget $30,849,638 (Principal $18,745,000, Interest $12,102,813, Other $1,825) versus actual $0; net budgeted $11,212 versus actual $1,576,169.

Food Service Fund (520): revenues budget $6,458,707 versus actual $115,931; expenditures budget $6,060,793 versus actual $87,811; net budgeted $397,914 versus actual $28,120.

Troy Career Center Fund (529): revenues and expenditures each budgeted $2,524,947, with July actuals of $147,240 on both sides (net zero), driven by Federal Sources.

Community Service Fund (530): revenues budget $1,970,000 (all local) versus actual $157,607; expenditures budget $2,101,071 versus actual $27,092; net budgeted $(131,071) versus actual $130,515.

Troy Preschool Fund (531): revenues budget $4,177,057 (Local $2,273,000, State $1,904,057) versus actual $100,073; expenditures budget $3,740,667 versus actual $52,752; net budgeted $436,390 versus actual $47,321.

Because the statement covers only the first month of the fiscal year, actual figures are a small fraction of annual budgets; state aid, most federal revenue, and the bulk of instructional and debt-service spending post later in the year. The report is presented to the Board as routine unaudited monthly financial information.

Correspondence from the Michigan Association of School Boards (MASB) placed before the Troy Board of Education, notifying it that MASB's 2024 Delegate Assembly will convene Thursday, October 24, 2024 at 7 p.m. at the Lansing Center in Lansing. The email, dated July 18, 2024, is sent by Cheryl Huffman, MASB Board Liaison, to Judy Holmes of the Troy district office, and carries a standard external-sender caution banner.

The Delegate Assembly is the body through which boards of education across Michigan decide MASB's positions on a wide variety of issues affecting education. The message asks the Troy board to certify its official voting delegates and alternates via an online form. It specifies that all delegates and alternates must be school board members, and that only delegates and alternates named by the board may offer motions and vote on issues, though all board members may speak on the issues and participate in debate. Participation is contingent on the district's 2024-2025 MASB dues being paid.

Delegates must be certified and submitted by Friday, October 4, 2024. Huffman notes that a companion notification is being sent to the board president and superintendent, and asks that the topic be added to the board's next meeting agenda. Contact information is provided (chuffman@masb.org; 517.327.5915), along with MASB's Lansing address at 1001 Centennial Way, Suite 400. The document is procedural, prompting a board action to name delegates.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Proposed amendment to the Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA) bylaws, presented with rationale for member-district consideration. The recommendation adds exception language to Article VI, Section 2 (Election of Board of Directors, Eligibility) allowing a director who is elected or appointed to another member district's board already represented on the OCSBA Board of Directors to complete their current term. The change addresses a conflict arising January 1, 2025, when an intermediate school district (ISD) trustee's expiring local (LEA) board term would otherwise force that director off the OCSBA board.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
Proposed OCSBA bylaws amendment with rationale (backup to the October 2024 bylaws ballot), recommending added exception language to Article VI, Section 2.

Recommendation
ADD exception language (shown in green) to the bylaws.

Article VI, Election of Board of Directors, Section 2 (Eligibility)
Any Member is eligible to be elected to the Association's Board of Directors; only one Member from each Member School District may serve on the Board at any given time.
Proposed Exception: If a Member of the Board of Directors is elected or appointed to another Member School District Board of Education already represented on the Board of Directors, that Director may complete their current term on the Board of Directors.

Rationale
- A conflict with OCSBA bylaws will occur on January 1, 2025.
- A newly elected ISD Board of Education trustee currently also serves on a LEA board (an eligible OCSBA board seat). When the LEA term expires 12/31/2024, the director would serve only on the ISD board, which is already represented on the OCSBA Board of Directors.
- Without the exception, OCSBA loses a director on January 1, 2025; OCSBA elections have shown too few active members willing to serve on the working board.
- If approved, two (2) ISD trustees remain on the OCSBA Board of Directors until their current terms end in June 2026, when the exception expires and only one ISD board member may serve.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
The substantive proposal underlying the October 2024 OCSBA member-district ballot: a recommended amendment to the bylaws of the Oakland County School Boards Association, presented together with its rationale. The recommendation is to ADD exception language (indicated as shown in green) to the bylaws governing the election of the Association's Board of Directors.

The relevant provision is Article VI, Election of Board of Directors, Section 2 (Eligibility), which currently provides that any Member is eligible to be elected to the Association's Board of Directors and that only one Member from each Member School District is allowed to serve on the Board at any given time. The proposed Exception reads: If a Member of the Board of Directors is elected or appointed to another Member School District Board of Education that is already represented on the Board of Directors, that Director may complete their current term on the Board of Directors.

The rationale explains that a conflict with the OCSBA bylaws will occur on January 1, 2025, and describes it specifically: a newly elected intermediate school district (ISD) Board of Education trustee currently also serves on a local education agency (LEA) board, which is an eligible seat on the OCSBA Board of Directors. However, when that LEA board term expires on 12/31/2024, the director will only serve on the ISD Board of Education, which is already represented on the OCSBA Board of Directors, creating the eligibility conflict under the existing one-member-per-district rule. The OCSBA Board of Directors recommends approval of the additional language to provide an exception in this rare situation, noting that the OCSBA Board of Directors is a working board and that OCSBA elections have repeatedly shown that not enough active OCSBA members are willing to serve on the Board of Directors.

The rationale sets out the consequences of the vote: if the member school districts do not approve the proposed exception, the OCSBA Board of Directors will lose a director on January 1, 2025. If the exception is approved, two (2) ISD trustees will remain on the OCSBA Board of Directors until their current Board of Directors terms end in June 2026; at the end of those terms the exception will expire, and only one Member from the ISD Board of Education will be allowed to serve on the OCSBA Board of Directors. This document is the explanatory companion to the ballot circulated to member districts (including Troy) on September 19, 2024, with voting open through October 31, 2024.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A staff presentation, "Staffing Process Update," delivered to the Troy Board of Education on October 1, 2024, outlining the district's hiring process and profiling the 2024 class of new hires. It describes a multi-stage pipeline — generalized job postings, screening via Applicant Central, recruitment and interview committees, and a building-level process ending with interviews by the assistant superintendents and superintendent and final Board approval. The 2024 class comprises 31 new teachers (3 TSD graduates; 14 with education beyond a bachelor's degree) and 9 new administrators (4 internal, 5 external), at a 14% diversity hiring rate.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
- Staff presentation titled "Staffing Process Update," dated October 1, 2024, given at the Troy Board of Education workshop.

Purpose
- Walk the board through the TSD hiring process and introduce the 2024 class of new employees.

Hiring pipeline
- Generalized openings posted via TSD, the Oakland Consortium, Indeed, MSBO, and similar channels.
- Screening committees (via Applicant Central): candidate profile/stakeholder surveys, structured screener interview, Applitrack Teacher/Admin Fit Assessment, verification of certification/endorsement, reference checks.
- Recruitment committees: consistent profile-based questions, TSD Elementary Teacher Job Fair, university recruitment fairs, diversity recruitment.
- Interview committees (admins plus department and building reps): writing prompt, required teaching/admin observation, background checks and fingerprinting, prior evaluations.
- Final interviews with the Assistant Superintendent/Director of Employee Services, Assistant Superintendent of Elementary/Secondary, and the Superintendent; contract offer; Board of Education final approval.
- Candidate pools by level: K-2 and 3-5; 6-8 and 9-12 by subject matter/specialty.

2024 class
- 31 new teachers (3 are TSD graduates; 14 have education beyond a bachelor's degree).
- 9 new administrators (4 internal, 5 external candidates).
- 14% diversity hiring rate for 2024.

Also referenced
- An Administrator Rubric.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose: Staff presentation titled "Staffing Process Update," dated October 1, 2024 and delivered at the Troy Board of Education workshop, walking the board through the district's hiring pipeline and introducing the 2024 cohort of new employees. The TSD hiring process is depicted as a series of committees and stages: generalized openings are posted to allow candidates to apply through channels including TSD, the Oakland Consortium, Indeed, and MSBO; screening committees operate via Applicant Central; and recruitment and interview committees (including administrators plus department and building representatives) evaluate candidates. Screening steps include candidate profile/stakeholder surveys, a structured screener interview, an Applitrack Teacher/Admin Fit Assessment, verification of certification and endorsement, general reference checks, and seeking diversity applicants when available. Recruitment activities include consistent interview questions geared to the teacher/admin candidate profile, the TSD Elementary Teacher Job Fair, attending university recruitment fairs in person and virtually, referring top candidates to Applicant Central, and inviting top job-fair candidates to a day of TSD professional learning. Interview committees look for evidence of profile characteristics, subject-matter knowledge, teaching qualities, a focus on students, and best practices; candidates respond to a writing prompt and must include a teaching or administrative observation, proof of certification and MTTC status if applicable, thorough reference and background checks with fingerprinting, previous evaluations, and other performance-based exercises. The building-level process culminates in interviews with the Assistant Superintendent/Director of Employee Services, the Assistant Superintendent of Elementary/Secondary, and the Superintendent, followed by determination of a contract offer and Board of Education final approval. Candidate pools are organized by level: K-2 and 3-5; 6-8 by subject matter/specialty; and 9-12 by subject matter/specialty. The presentation also references an Administrator Rubric. The closing "2024 Class: Who Are They?" slide reports 31 new TSD teachers, 3 of whom are TSD graduates; 14 teachers with educational experience beyond a bachelor's degree; 9 new TSD administrators (4 internal and 5 external candidates); and a 14% diversity hiring rate for 2024. This is the PDF version of the slide deck.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A proposed amendment to the Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA) bylaws, presented with rationale in the materials for the October 15, 2024 regular board meeting. It adds exception language to Article VI, Section 2 (Eligibility) allowing a director who joins another already-represented member district's board to finish their current OCSBA term. The change resolves a conflict arising January 1, 2025, when an ISD trustee's LEA board term expires; without it the OCSBA Board of Directors would lose a member. The exception expires when the affected terms end in June 2026.

What it is
Proposed bylaws amendment (with rationale) from the Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA), included in the Troy Board's October 15, 2024 regular meeting materials for member-district approval.

The change
Adds 'exception' language to Article VI, Election of Board of Directors, Section 2 (Eligibility). The existing rule allows only one member from each member school district to serve on the OCSBA Board of Directors at any time. The exception provides that if a director is later elected or appointed to another member district's board of education that is already represented on the Board of Directors, that director may complete their current term.

Why
- A conflict with OCSBA bylaws arises January 1, 2025.
- A newly elected ISD Board of Education trustee currently also serves on a LEA board (an eligible OCSBA seat). When the LEA term expires 12/31/2024, that director would serve only on the ISD board, which is already represented.
- The OCSBA Board is a 'working board,' and elections have repeatedly shown too few active members are willing to serve.

Consequences
- If member districts do NOT approve, OCSBA loses a director on January 1, 2025.
- If approved, two ISD trustees remain on the Board of Directors until their current terms end in June 2026, at which point the exception expires and the one-member-per-ISD limit resumes.

Action
OCSBA recommends approval of the added language by its member school districts.

The proposed exception reads: if a member of the Board of Directors is elected or appointed to another member school district Board of Education that is already represented on the Board of Directors, that director may complete their current term on the Board of Directors.

Rationale. A conflict with the OCSBA bylaws will occur on January 1, 2025. The specific situation: a newly elected Intermediate School District (ISD) Board of Education trustee currently also serves on a Local Education Agency (LEA) board, which is an eligible seat on the OCSBA Board of Directors. What it is
Consent agenda item 5.D. for the Troy School District Board of Education regular meeting of October 15, 2024, appointing local parent representatives to the Special Education Parent Advisory Committee (PAC).

Background
Under the Michigan Administrative Rules for Special Education (MARSE), each intermediate school district (ISD) must have a PAC made up of representatives from its local districts. Members serve staggered three-year terms so that a majority of experienced members always remain, and the ISD must ensure appropriate representation across all disability categories. Each local representative must be approved by the local district's Board of Education.

Recommendation
Sara Smotherman, Director of Special Education, recommended two parent representatives:
- Reem Sater Komives - Hamilton Elementary School
- Kate Wharton - Schroeder Elementary School

Action
The suggested resolution asks the Board to appoint both individuals as representatives to the Oakland County Special Education Parent Advisory Committee (PAC), with recorded Yes/No votes and mover/supporter lines left blank on the draft.

Purpose
Fulfill the district's MARSE obligation to provide Board-approved parent representation on the ISD-level special education advisory committee.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Consent agenda item 5.D., presented to the Troy School District Board of Education at its regular meeting on October 15, 2024, concerns the appointment of local parent representatives to the Special Education Parent Advisory Committee (PAC).

Regulatory basis: The item explains that under the Michigan Administrative Rules for Special Education (MARSE), each intermediate school district (ISD) must maintain a Special Education Parent Advisory Committee. The committee is composed of representatives from local districts who serve three-year terms, with terms staggered to assure that a majority of experienced members remain on the committee at any time. The ISD is also required to ensure appropriate representation for all disability categories. Critically, each representative from a local district must be approved by that local school district's Board of Education, which is the reason this appointment comes before the Troy Board.

Recommendation: Sara Smotherman, the district's Director of Special Education, recommended two parent representatives for the District. The Board is asked to appoint Reem Sater Komives, associated with Hamilton Elementary School, and Kate Wharton, associated with Schroeder Elementary School, as representatives to the PAC (identified in the resolution as the Oakland County Special Education Parent Advisory Committee).

Recommended action and resolution: The recommended action is acceptance of the suggested resolution. The draft resolution reads, in substance, 'BE IT THEREFORE RESOLVED that the Board of Education takes action to appoint Reem Sater Komives and Kate Wharton as representatives to the Oakland County Special Education Parent Advisory Committee (PAC).' The draft leaves the mover, supporter, and the YES and NO vote tallies blank, to be completed when the Board acts on the measure. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Attached to agenda item 8.A. for the Troy School District Board of Education regular meeting of October 15, 2024, is an award recommendation letter from Barton Malow Builders (26500 American Dr., Southfield, MI 48034), the construction manager, addressed to Dan Trudel, Assistant Superintendent of Business Services, Troy School District (4420 Livernois Rd, Troy, MI 48098). The letter is dated September 24, 2024, and concerns Bid Package #3B (BP#3B) for the New Smith Middle School project.

Bidding process: Bid proposals were received and read publicly on July 30, 2024, and August 8, 2024. Barton Malow reviewed the proposals with the Project Architect/Engineer, TMP Architecture Inc. The project was advertised on the state website for a total of five and a half weeks, collecting 38 bids across the affected categories. The scope covers New Smith Middle School work not previously bid earlier in the year, and this recommendation represents the majority of the remaining categories not interviewed or decided before the last award recommendation.

Recommended contractor awards: Metal Wall Panels (3B.4) to Silverline Contracting for $2,345,000; Painting (3B.10) to R&G Painting Home Improvement LLC for $314,000; Acoustical Wall Units (3B.11) to Clark Contracting Services for $374,800; Casework (3B.13) to Division 6 Fabrication & Installation for $973,133; Food Service Equipment (3B.14) to Stafford-Smith, Inc. for $751,821; Structured Cabling (3B.23) to Amcomm Telecommunications Inc. for $263,900; Earthwork (3B.24) to Cortis Brothers Trucking & Excavating for $2,949,700; Landscape (3B.25) to Heritage and Company, Inc. for $1,148,035; Gymnasium Equipment (3B.16) to C & M Associates, Inc. for $126,965; and Gymnasium Equipment - Bleachers (3B.16) to Interkal Inc. for $155,758. The total contractor direct cost is $9,403,112, with an 8% contingency of $752,249, for a total construction cost of $10,155,361.

Bid exceptions: The low bidders for Structured Cabling and Acoustical Wall Units did not submit complete bids and are not recommended; instead the second-low acoustical bidder, Clark Contracting Services, and the fourth-low cabling bidder, Amcomm Telecommunications, were interviewed, confirmed they included all identified work, and are recommended. In the signage category no bidder submitted a complete and qualified bid; the fourth-low bidder, DMP Signs, offered a complete bid but with an alternate (non-specified) product still under review for equivalence, so the category will either be awarded to DMP Signs or rebid. Work related to the traffic signal at the Livernois intersection remains in design and will be bid later; the engineer's estimate for it is carried in the projected cost.

Cumulative and projected costs: The total construction cost including contingency across all prior award recommendations is $54,424,961. Including the estimated remaining work, the projected cost of the building is about $55,500,000. Additional technology and security work will be bid separately under a budget distinct from the building's construction. The attached bid tabulation also lists bidders in categories such as Masonry (low bidder Arisco Contracting Group, Inc. at $4,859,222, with other bidders up to J&J Construction Company at $5,880,485), General Trades (low bidder Graham Construction at $1,276,700), and Carpentry (Clark Construction Company at $3,889,600). Purchasing Department letter of recommendation (agenda item 8.B.) to the Troy School District Board of Education, dated October 14, 2024, for new cafeteria tables at Leonard Elementary School.

Replace existing, aged cafeteria tables at Leonard Elementary with 20 oval tables, each surrounded by four benches, used for daily lunch periods, before/after-school care, and other events.

Award to Great Lakes Furniture Supply, Inc. at $48,530.00. Although School Specialty is cheaper, Great Lakes is recommended for longevity: its tables use a strut lifting system expected to work for 20 years, versus torsion-bar/spring tables that fatigue in 7-9 years.

A Purchasing Department letter of recommendation supports agenda item 8.B. at the Troy School District Board of Education regular meeting of October 15, 2024. Dated October 14, 2024, it is a memorandum from Jennifer Vente, Purchasing Coordinator (1140 Rankin, Troy, MI 48083-6003; Ivente@troy.k12.mi.us; 248/823-4078), to Aurel Malutan, Finance Director, Business Services. The header also references Superintendent of Schools Richard M. Machesky, Ed.D., and Daniel Trudel, Assistant Superintendent, Business Services.

Purpose and scope: The district requests a new cafeteria table purchase to replace the existing cafeteria tables at Leonard Elementary School due to their age and condition. The purchase is for 20 oval tables, each with four benches, to be used primarily for daily lunch periods, before- and after-school care programs, and other events and functions throughout the school year.

Pricing and quotes: Pricing was obtained from various purchasing cooperatives, including Sourcewell-SICO and AEPA-OCSPO, using bond funds under account 423-008-456-0000-00-6410. Three vendor quotes were received: School Specialty at $43,498.80 (dated 10/08/24); Great Lakes Furniture Supply, Inc. at $48,530.00 (dated 10/11/24); and School Outfitters at $58,997.60 (dated 10/14/24). The applicable cooperative contracts are cited as AEPA Coop Contract IFB022-A and Sourcewell Coop #091423-SICO.

Recommendation and rationale: Even though School Specialty offered a cheaper price, Purchasing recommends awarding to Great Lakes Furniture Supply, Inc. because of the superior quality and lasting longevity of its tables (described as a 'workhorse of a table'). The recommended tables are equipped with a strut system for lifting and lowering, so that in 20 years the tables will still lift and lower as designed, whereas tables with torsion bars or springs are said to fatigue after 7-9 years, making them hard to raise and lower. The recommended amount is $48,530.00. The letter asks that the Board accept the recommendation for approval and offers to answer any questions, and closes noting the district's status as an Equal Opportunity/Affirmative Action Employer.

Transmittal email included in the Troy School District board packet documenting a pending vote of member districts on a proposed amendment to the bylaws of the Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA). The message was forwarded by the OCSBA Board on Wednesday, October 9, 2024 (11:36 a.m.) as a friendly reminder that the voting window remained open until October 31st, and it reproduces the original notice sent by the OCSBA Board (ocsbaboard@ocsba-mi.org) on Thursday, September 19, 2024 (1:09 p.m.). The email carries a standard external-sender caution banner.

The substance explains that proposed resolutions and changes to the Association's bylaws require a vote of its member districts, and that OCSBA is submitting a proposed amendment for consideration. Under the OCSBA bylaws, member districts must be given at least forty (40) calendar days to vote; therefore the window for each board of education to vote closes on Thursday, October 31, 2024. Two documents are attached and referenced: the proposed amendments to the OCSBA bylaws with the rationale for the change, and one (1) ballot for the proposed amendments (files named 2024 Proposed Bylaws Language with Rationale and Ballot - Bylaws Vote - Oct2024).

Recipients are directed to contact Stefanie Crane at 248-835-5062 or scrane@clarkston.k12.mi.us, or Amy Hochkammer at 248-229-8405 or ahochkammer@birmingham.k12.mi.us, with questions regarding the proposed changes. The message thanks the committee members who worked on the proposal: Marc Siegler (Walled Lake), Stefanie Crane (Clarkston), and Marc Katz (Oakland Schools). It is signed by the Board of Directors of the Oakland County School Boards Association. The email is procedural, serving to alert the Troy board that action (a recorded YES/NO vote on the amendment) is required before the deadline; the underlying substantive change is detailed in the accompanying rationale document, which addresses an eligibility conflict arising on January 1, 2025 for directors who serve on both an intermediate school district (ISD) board and a local education agency (LEA) board.

2024 Member District Ballot for proposed amendments to the Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA) bylaws, to be completed by each member board of education.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
The official 2024 Member District Ballot issued by the Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA) for a vote on proposed amendments to the Association bylaws. An introductory note explains that the OCSBA Resolution and Bylaws committee reviews the Association bylaws annually and recommends amendments as needed, and that once proposed amendment(s) are reviewed by the Board of Directors they are transmitted to member districts for consideration.

The ballot quotes the governing bylaw provisions. OCSBA Bylaws Article XVI, Section 1 (Amendments) states that the bylaws may be altered or amended by the vote of the Member School Districts; the Board of Directors will provide a written ballot with the proposed amendment(s) to each Member School District, giving at least a forty (40) day period in which to vote, and each Member School District will have one (1) vote. Article III, Section 2 provides that Member School District votes shall be recorded upon receipt of the completed resolution or ballot indicating the vote of the district's Trustees, and must be received prior to the stated deadline.

Regarding the voting period, the document states that the proposed amendment(s), a rationale for the change, and a written ballot were transmitted to every Member and all Member School District Executive Assistants on September 19, 2024, and that completed ballots must be received no later than 5:00 PM on Thursday, October 31, 2024. It emphasizes that the ballot must be completed, signed, and returned to OCSBAboard@ocsba-mi.org before the deadline or the district's vote cannot be counted.

The voting instrument itself asks: DOES THE BOARD OF EDUCATION APPROVE THE PROPOSED AMENDMENT(S) TO THE ASSOCIATION BYLAWS? It provides fill-in blanks for the district name and the meeting date (20__) and two checkboxes: YES, the Board approves the proposed amendment(s) to the bylaws as presented; or NO, the Board does not approve. A certification line reads that the signer hereby certifies the foregoing is a true and correct record of the vote by the Board of Education, with a choice of signatory role (Board Secretary, or Executive Assistant to the Board and Superintendent) and lines for printed name and signature. Instructions repeat that the completed and signed ballot must be emailed to OCSBAboard@ocsba-mi.org no later than 5:00 PM on Thursday, October 31, 2024. Contacts for questions are Stefanie Crane (scrane@clarkston.k12.mi.us) and Amy Hochkammer (ahochkammer@birmingham.k12.mi.us, 248-229-8405). The ballot is the action instrument corresponding to the OCSBA bylaws amendment concerning Board of Directors eligibility for members serving on both ISD and LEA boards.

Individual programs (allocated approximately equal to expended): CRF $6,501K; ESSER I $246K; ESSER II $1,675K/$1,674K; ESSER II Equalization (State) $5,036K; ESSER III $1,895K; ESSER III Equalization $12,385K; GEER $22K; GEER II $53K; and ARP-IDEA $598K.

Governmental funds (year ended June 30, 2024): The General Fund reported revenue of $194,996,044 against expenditures of $191,469,703, an excess of $3,526,341, plus other financing sources of $627,865, for a net change in fund balance of $4,154,206; fund balance grew from $32,620,321 to $36,774,527. The 2023 Capital Projects Fund had revenue of $10,180,060 and expenditures of $20,963,191 (net -$10,783,131), reducing its fund balance from $188,680,666 to $177,897,535 as bond-funded construction proceeded. Total Nonmajor Funds had revenue of $55,019,407 and expenditures of $56,585,368 (net -$1,565,961), ending at $14,821,514.

General Fund revenue detail: $194,996,044 total -- State source $129,832,155 (67%), Local $44,635,678 (23%), Interdistrict $12,311,867 (6%), and Federal $8,216,344 (4%). Viewed by foundation components: State Portion of Foundation Allowance $87,516,980 (45%), Other State and Local $58,604,764 (30%), Property Taxes $40,657,956 (21%), and Federal $8,216,344 (4%).

General Fund expenditures ($191,469,703): by object -- Salaries and Employee Benefits $153,754,214 (80%), Purchased Services $27,888,301 (15%), Supplies $7,050,320 (4%), and Other Expenses $2,776,868 (1%). By function -- Direct Instruction 65.24%, Indirect Instruction 13.87%, Operations and Maintenance 7.52%, School Administration 4.98%, General Administration and Business Services 2.39%, Pupil Transportation 2.27%, Central Services 1.98%, Athletics 1.35%, Debt Service 0.31%, and Community Services 0.12%. The presentation notes the Oakland County average for Direct Instruction in FY23 was 60.02%, versus Troy's 65.24%.

Enrollment and foundation allowance: Student population was 12,177 in 2008-09, peaked around 13,111 in 2019-20, and was 12,359 for 2024-25; the per-pupil foundation allowance rose from $9,275 (2008-09) to $10,394 in both 2023-24 and 2024-25. Among 13 listed Oakland County districts for 2023-24, Troy's $10,394 ranked sixth, below Bloomfield Hills ($13,443), Birmingham ($13,363), Southfield ($12,410), Lamphere ($11,868), and Farmington ($11,484), and above West Bloomfield ($10,235), Royal Oak ($10,197), Novi ($9,918), Walled Lake ($9,754), and Rochester, Waterford, and Huron Valley (each $9,608).

Fund balance history: Over the ten years ending June 30, 2024, General Fund fund balance grew from $20,701K (15.08% of expenditures) in FY2015 to $36,774K (19.21%) in FY2024, equivalent to about 10 weeks or 69 days of operations; the statewide average fund balance as a percent of expenditures for FY2023 was 21.86%. The presentation's purpose was to report the audit results and the district's financial position to the board.

The report affirms that Troy School District is an independent reporting entity fully meeting the criteria established by the Governmental Accounting Standards Board (GASB), that all district funds are included, and that the district has no component units. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
The independent auditor's 'Report to the Board of Education' for Troy School District, a governance communication accompanying the audit of the district's basic financial statements as of and for the year ended June 30, 2024. It was presented at the Board of Education Workshop on November 12, 2024 (agenda item 2.a) and is dated October 28, 2024. The letter thanks Mr. Dan Trudel, Mr. Aurel Malutan, and the entire business office for their assistance and preparedness during the audit, noting that audit preparation is carried out in addition to staff's normal daily activities.

The report is organized into three parts: Results of the Audit (pages 1-4), Other Recommendations and Observations (pages 5-6), and Informational Items (pages 7-19).

Under 'Our Responsibility Under U.S. Generally Accepted Auditing Standards,' the auditor explains, per an engagement letter dated June 17, 2024, that its responsibility is to express an opinion about whether the financial statements prepared by management with the Board's oversight are fairly presented, in all material respects, in conformity with U.S. generally accepted accounting principles. The audit does not relieve management or the Board of their responsibilities and provides reasonable, but not absolute, assurance that the statements are free of material misstatement. Internal control was considered solely to design audit procedures, not to express an opinion on its effectiveness.

The audit was also conducted in accordance with Government Auditing Standards issued by the Comptroller General of the United States, under which the auditor must communicate matters such as compliance with laws, regulations, contracts, and grant agreements; instances of error or fraud; illegal acts applicable to government agencies; and significant deficiencies in internal control. A separate letter dated October 28, 2024 addresses the auditor's consideration of the district's internal control over financial reporting and its tests of compliance.

Regarding planned scope and timing, the audit was performed according to the scope and timing previously communicated at a planning meeting on August 27, 2024.

Significant Audit Findings - Qualitative Aspects of Accounting Practices: Management is responsible for selecting and applying appropriate accounting policies, described in Note 2 to the financial statements. No new accounting policies were adopted, and the application of existing policies was not changed during 2024. The auditor noted no transactions entered into during the year for which there is a lack of authoritative guidance or consensus, and no significant transactions recognized in the financial statements in a different period than when they occurred. The most sensitive accounting estimates affecting the financial statements were the district's proportionate share of the MPSERS (Michigan Public School Employees' Retirement System) net pension liability and the net asset for other postemployment benefit (OPEB) plans recorded on the government-wide statements, related to GASB Statement Nos. 68 and 75. The report invites the Board to direct any questions about its comments to the auditor. The extracted text is truncated before the detailed recommendations, observations, and informational items in the later pages.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
The Troy School District Federal Awards Supplemental Information as of June 30, 2024 - the district's federal 'single audit' report - presented at the Board of Education Workshop on November 12, 2024 (agenda item 2.a). The document comprises a series of independent auditor's reports and schedules prepared to meet the requirements of the Uniform Guidance.

Contents and page references: Report on Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards Required by the Uniform Guidance (page 1); Report on Internal Control Over Financial Reporting and on Compliance and Other Matters Based on an Audit of Financial Statements Performed in Accordance with Government Auditing Standards (pages 2-3); Report on Compliance for Each Major Federal Program and Report on Internal Control Over Compliance Required by the Uniform Guidance (pages 4-6); Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards (pages 7-10); Reconciliation of Basic Financial Statements Federal Revenue with Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards (page 11); Notes to Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards (page 12); and Schedule of Findings and Questioned Costs (page 13).

In the first report, the auditor states that it audited the financial statements of the governmental activities, each major fund, and the aggregate remaining fund information of Troy School District as of and for the year ended June 30, 2024, and issued its report thereon dated October 28, 2024, which contained an unmodified opinion on the financial statements. The accompanying schedule of expenditures of federal awards and the reconciliation of federal revenue are presented for purposes of additional analysis as required by the Uniform Guidance and are not a required part of the basic financial statements. This information, the responsibility of management, was derived from and relates directly to the underlying accounting records and was subjected to auditing procedures, including comparing and reconciling it to those records. In the auditor's opinion, the schedule of expenditures of federal awards and the reconciliation are fairly stated in all material respects in relation to the financial statements as a whole.

The second report addresses internal control over financial reporting. In planning and performing the audit, the auditor considered the district's internal control to design appropriate audit procedures but not to express an opinion on the effectiveness of that internal control, and it does not express such an opinion. The report defines a deficiency in internal control, a material weakness (a deficiency or combination of deficiencies such that there is a reasonable possibility that a material misstatement will not be prevented, or detected and corrected, on a timely basis), and a significant deficiency (less severe than a material weakness but important enough to merit attention by those charged with governance). The consideration of internal control was for the limited purpose described and was not designed to identify all deficiencies that might be material weaknesses or significant deficiencies. The extracted text is truncated before the specific compliance conclusions, major-program determinations, and the contents of the Schedule of Findings and Questioned Costs, so no dollar amounts of federal expenditures or specific findings appear in the available text.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A Board of Education workshop presentation titled 'Exploring Our Data Story' (subtitled 'A Tale of Achievement'), delivered on November 12, 2024. Its stated objectives are to review district goals, provide context to enhance understanding of data, and share how data is used to drive the district's systems and processes. The presentation frames the district's four goal areas as: (1) Early Childhood to Career, (2) Equity & Well-Being, (3) Deep Learning, and (4) Building Capacity.

It distinguishes summative from formative assessment. Summative (district-level) measures include M-STEP (grades 3-7), PSAT 8 / SAT 11, and College Board Advanced Placement. Formative (classroom-level) measures include Fountas & Pinnell (K-5), Bridges Math (K-5), Common Lit (ELA 6-12), and NWEA Math (grade 6 to Algebra 1), along with exit data and the TCCHS graduation rate. The presentation acknowledges limitations of summative data (useful for cohort tracking and comparative insights, but lacking granularity for specific performance insights).

Multi-year proficiency figures compare Troy School District (TSD) to Oakland Schools (OS) and the State across 2018-19, 2021-22, 2022-23, and 2023-24. M-STEP ELA grades 3-7: TSD 74.3, 68.9, 67, 65.6; OS 53.6, 50.1, 49.7, 49.4; State 44.3, 40.7, 40.7, 40.5. M-STEP Math grades 3-7: TSD 70.1, 64.7, 65.7, 67.4; OS 48.9, 42.6, 43.7, 45; State 38.7, 33.3, 34.7, 35.6. The presentation also breaks out elementary (grades 3-5) versus middle-school (grades 6 & 7) M-STEP ELA and Math, and shows M-STEP Science and Social Studies by elementary/middle/high levels for 2021-22 through 2023-24.

PSAT 8 EBRW (Evidence-Based Reading & Writing): TSD 87.1, 81, 85.6, 84.2; Oakland Schools 70.3, 67, 68.4, 71.4; State 61.9, 59.7, 59.7, 64.5. PSAT 8 Math: TSD 75.1, 67.5, 69, 64.3; OS 52.5, 44.6, 45.5, 42.3; State 41.4, 36.2, 36.2, 32.6. SAT EBRW: TSD 82.9, 75.3, 76.9, 77.3; OS 62.9, 59, 59.3, 59.6; State 55.3, 51.6, 52.2, 51.3. SAT Math: TSD 73.6, 61.6, 61.3, 59.5; OS 46.7, 39.3, 38.9, 35.7; State 36.3, 30, 29.9, 26.3. SAT overall performance is also charted across 2018-19 through 2023-24.

SAT results are further broken out by the district's two high schools (labeled AHS and THS) for 2021-22 through 2023-24 (percent met or exceeded expectations): SAT Total - AHS 51.1, 53, 50.3; THS 67.5, 70, 67.2. SAT EBRW - AHS 70.1, 76, 72.7; THS 81.7, 81.5, 82.5. SAT Math - AHS 53.5, 54.6, 53.8; THS 70.6, 71.8, 69.2.

The latter half addresses using data to inform instruction through the district's Multi-Tiered System of Supports (MTSS): MTSS decision-making, dedicated MTSS time, building data and trends, progress monitoring of students on plans, and inclusion of students with IEPs in scheduling discussions. Formative tools discussed include the Fountas & Pinnell Benchmark (by grade level), a Math Benchmark (by grade), the Math Recovery Assessment (elementary universal screener with diagnostic follow-up by math specialists), an NWEA universal screener newly established for middle-school mathematics (enabling participation in a third-party study with Illustrative Mathematics), and the Common Lit assessment used as a baseline to identify needs, drive instruction, monitor growth, and support student goal-setting. The presentation cites a partnership with NSK12 to evaluate supports and structures for students in English Language Development (ELD), Special Education, and other areas, and references ongoing professional learning (e.g., an October 31-November 1 'Trailguide'). It closes with 'Reading Between the Lines / Next Steps,' identifying district improvement needs (screen-and-diagnose to improve the MTSS process, formation of work groups to build capacity, shared ownership of the MTSS process) alongside celebrations such as investment in early childhood.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A report from the district's independent auditors to the Board of Education of Troy School District, delivered alongside the audit of the district's basic financial statements as of and for the year ended June 30, 2024. The letter is dated October 28, 2024 and is organized into three parts: Results of the Audit (pages 1-4), Other Recommendations and Observations (pages 5-6), and Informational Items (pages 7-19).

Auditor responsibility and scope: As set out in the engagement letter dated June 17, 2024, the auditors' responsibility is to express an opinion on whether the financial statements prepared by management (with the Board's oversight) are fairly presented, in all material respects, in conformity with U.S. generally accepted accounting principles, obtaining reasonable but not absolute assurance that the statements are free of material misstatement. The audit does not relieve management or the Board of their responsibilities. In considering the district's internal control, the auditors did so solely to design audit procedures and not to express an opinion on the effectiveness of internal control. The audit was also conducted in accordance with Government Auditing Standards issued by the Comptroller General of the United States, under which the auditors must communicate matters including compliance with laws, regulations, contracts, and grant agreements, instances of error or fraud, illegal acts, and significant deficiencies in internal control; a separate letter dated October 28, 2024 addresses the consideration of internal control over financial reporting and tests of compliance.

Planning and timing: The audit was performed according to the planned scope and timing previously communicated in a planning meeting on August 27, 2024.

Significant audit findings: Regarding the qualitative aspects of accounting practices, management is responsible for selecting and using appropriate accounting policies, which are described in Note 2 to the financial statements. No new accounting policies were adopted, and the application of existing policies was not changed during 2024. The auditors noted no transactions entered into during the year for which there is a lack of authoritative guidance or consensus, and no significant transactions recognized in a period different from when they occurred. Accounting estimates are described as an integral part of the statements, based on management's knowledge and assumptions; the most sensitive estimates affecting the financial statements were the district's share of the MPSERS net pension liability and the net asset for the other postemployment benefit (OPEB) plans recorded on the government-wide statements under GASB Statement Nos. 68 and 75.

Acknowledgements: The auditors express thanks to Mr. Dan Trudel, Mr. Aurel Malutan, and the entire business office for their assistance and preparedness during the audit, noting that preparing for the audit is carried out in addition to staff's normal daily activities, and invite questions on any of the comments in the report.

The Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards and the reconciliation are presented for purposes of additional analysis as required by the Uniform Guidance and are not a required part of the basic financial statements; the information is the responsibility of management and was derived from the underlying accounting records. Having subjected this information to the auditing procedures applied in the audit of the basic financial statements and certain additional procedures, the auditors express the opinion that the schedule and its reconciliation are fairly stated in all material respects in relation to the financial statements as a whole.

Internal control and compliance: In the Government Auditing Standards report, the auditors describe considering the district's internal control over financial reporting as a basis for designing audit procedures appropriate in the circumstances for expressing opinions on the financial statements, but not for the purpose of expressing an opinion on the effectiveness of internal control, and accordingly they do not express such an opinion. The report defines the relevant terms: a deficiency in internal control exists when the design or operation of a control does not allow management or employees, in the normal course of performing their assigned functions, to prevent, or detect and correct, misstatements on a timely basis; a material weakness is a deficiency, or combination of deficiencies, such that there is a reasonable possibility that a material misstatement will not be prevented, or detected and corrected, on a timely basis; and a significant deficiency is less severe than a material weakness yet important enough to merit attention by those charged with governance. The excerpt notes that the consideration of internal control was for the limited purpose described and was not designed to identify all deficiencies that might be material weaknesses or significant deficiencies.
